title: T1001.003 — Data Obfuscation - Protocol or Service Impersonation
subtitle: A step-by-step animation of an implant that hides its C2 as a jQuery download, plus the defender signals at each step.

steps.title: Profile
steps.caption: The implant loads its traffic profile. The profile is a small config that defines which headers to send, which URLs to use, and the timing of each request.
steps.defender: nothing is on the wire yet; sandbox detonation can dump the profile.

steps.title: Fake fetch
steps.caption: The implant sends GET /js/jquery-3.3.1.min.js to a server that is not a real CDN. The path and filename match a file that millions of sites load.
steps.defender: check the Host header - a real page would use a known CDN domain.

steps.title: Task in body
steps.caption: The reply claims to be JavaScript, but the body also carries encoded task data for the implant.
steps.defender: hash the response body and compare it with the public jQuery release hash.

steps.title: Form POST
steps.caption: The implant sends the task results as POST /submit.php , pretending to be a browser form submission with a Chrome user-agent string.
steps.defender: a user-agent says “browser”, but the timing and rhythm say “implant”.

steps.title: SOC view
steps.caption: The SOC console ingests netflow and proxy records. URL allow-lists and web-category filters pass the traffic as harmless “web” traffic.
steps.defender: coarse filters alone cannot catch this technique.

steps.title: JA3 alert
steps.caption: The SOC tool computes a JA3 hash of the TLS handshake. The fingerprint does not match any real browser, so the “Chrome” user-agent becomes a red flag.
steps.defender: JA3 plus user-agent mismatch is a high-value signal.

steps.title: Header order
steps.caption: Zeek records show an HTTP header order and casing that no Chrome build uses. Attackers can copy header values, but order and casing are hard to fake perfectly.
steps.defender: baseline real browsers, then alert on order deviations.

steps.title: Respond
steps.caption: The SOC blocks the fake CDN domain at the firewall, adds a JA3 detection rule, and compares library bodies against known hashes. The analyst isolates the victim PC with the EDR tool.
steps.defender: containment first, then hunt for the same fingerprint fleet-wide.
